title: Would You Build This Yourself or Buy a Managed Service?
summary: Tests whether you weigh differentiation, operational burden, and total cost concretely for the component in question, instead of defaulting to build or buy reflexively.

slides.markdown:
The interviewer asks: **"would you build this yourself, or use a managed service?"** It's testing whether you weigh differentiation, long-term operational burden, and total cost concretely for this specific component — not whether you reflexively favor "build" (control) or "buy" (speed).

A strong answer names which of those factors actually drives the call here, rather than reciting a general build-vs-buy philosophy that would apply to any component equally.

Ask: is this component core to the product's actual differentiation, or is it commodity infrastructure that every competitor also needs? And what's the team's real capacity to *operate* something it builds, long-term — not just the one-time cost to ship a first version.

Both questions matter because the honest cost of "build" is rarely the initial implementation; it's the years of patching, scaling, and on-call that follow. A team that can ship a feature in a sprint may still be unable to absorb owning it forever.

Buy commodity or undifferentiated pieces; build only where the component is core to what actually makes this product distinct from competitors.

The test for "core" isn't "do we do this a lot" — it's "would customers choose us over a competitor because of how well we do this specific thing." A payments system's fraud-detection model is often core; its message queue almost never is, even though both are used constantly.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: commodity infrastructure vs the differentiator
slides.markdown:
| | Buy | Build |
|---|---|---|
| Example | A managed queue (SQS), managed search (Elasticsearch Service) | A proprietary recommendation engine that is the actual product |
| Why | Commodity infrastructure — every company needs one, none differentiates on it | This *is* what makes the product distinct from competitors |
| Ongoing cost if wrong | Paying for flexibility you'll never use | Operating something core with mediocre in-house expertise |

**How to decide:** ask whether the component is something users would notice and prefer you *for*, specifically — if not, it's commodity, and buying frees engineering time for the part that is.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: a 15-person startup considering a proprietary queue
slides.markdown:
A 15-person startup considers building its own message queue for "full control." The honest total cost isn't the build time — it's the ongoing operational burden: patching, scaling, and on-call for the queue itself, on top of the initial build.

A team that size can't absorb that cost without pulling time away from the actual product. Buying is the right call here not because building a queue is impossible, but because of what it would cost everywhere else — every hour spent operating a homegrown queue is an hour not spent on the product's differentiator.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: the counter-case where building wins
slides.markdown:
The counter-case: a company whose entire value proposition is search relevance builds its own ranking system rather than using an off-the-shelf managed search product. The ranking logic *is* the differentiation — not commodity infrastructure sitting around it.

This is the same reasoning as the startup's queue, applied to the opposite conclusion: the question is never "is this hard to build" or "do we use it a lot," it's whether this specific piece is what customers are actually choosing the product for.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
Buying trades long-term flexibility and unit economics at scale for speed and reduced operational burden now. At high enough volume, a managed service's per-unit cost can exceed what an in-house equivalent would cost to run — which is exactly why some companies migrate from bought to built later, not because buying was wrong initially.

That migration is a deliberate, re-evaluated decision made with today's constraints and today's scale, not evidence the original buy call was a mistake made in ignorance.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: the managed service is missing a feature you need
slides.markdown:
Follow-up: "the managed service doesn't support a feature you need — do you still buy it?" Check whether the missing feature is a genuine hard blocker or a workaround-able gap.

A hard blocker on a capability that's actually part of your differentiation tips toward building instead. A minor gap on otherwise-commodity infrastructure usually doesn't — a workaround, or accepting the limitation, is cheaper than taking on the entire operational burden of an in-house replacement for one missing feature.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: the managed service is now your biggest cost line
slides.markdown:
Follow-up: "you bought a managed service two years ago and now it's your biggest infra cost line — was that the wrong call?" Not necessarily. It may have been correct for that stage, when speed mattered more than unit cost, and the correct call *now* is a deliberate migration evaluated against today's constraints.

Calling the original decision wrong with hindsight conflates two different questions — "was it right given what we knew and needed then" and "is it still right given what we know and need now." Both can have different, individually correct answers.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: building for hypothetical future flexibility
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** defaulting to "build" for everything because "we might need custom behavior someday."

**Why it's wrong:** this pays an ongoing operational tax — patching, scaling, on-call — for flexibility that, in most cases, is never actually used. The cost is paid every day; the benefit is speculative and may never materialize.

**Correct model:** only build where the component is core to differentiation today, or where a hard, named blocker on a managed alternative already exists — not for a future need you can't yet point to.

Buy commodity infrastructure; build only what's core to the product's actual differentiation. Justify the call with the specific component — not a general build-vs-buy philosophy — and weigh the honest total cost of building, which is dominated by long-term operational burden, not initial implementation.

Be ready to explain a missing-feature blocker (hard blocker on a differentiator tips toward build) and a cost-line reversal two years later (a deliberate re-evaluation, not proof the original call was wrong).
